meeting_header: Date: 2026-11-19 14:00 PST | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Evan Park (Redwood AE), Noor Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Kim (Redwood Solutions), Maj. Thomas Reed (Stratus CTO), Dr. Lina Chen (Stratus Security Architect), Sarah Morales (IT Ops), Carlos Vega (Procurement)
summary: Discovery focused on on-prem, air-gapped deployment requirements for a defense contractor. Key concerns: offline model updates, hardware procurement lead times, KMS/HSM integration, FIPS/STIG compliance, audit logs and SIEM integration, network segregation, and fallback/rollout strategies. Redwood to send security docs, hardware sizing, and schedule a deeper architecture call.
transcript:
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 45 minutes. Appreciate you making time. Quick intros — I'll pass to Noor for the technical overview after we do a quick round.
[00:12] Thomas: Thanks, Evan. Thomas Reed, CTO at Stratus Defense. Uh, we run quite a few classified-ish workloads so the, the air-gap thing is kind of central.
[00:20] Dr. Chen: Lina Chen, security architect. We'll be looking at FIPS requirements, STIG alignment, and how updates get into an isolated environment.
[00:28] Sarah: Sarah Morales, IT Ops, I'll be the day-to-day on build and ops. We have strict change control.
[00:33] Evan: Great thanks. Noor, over to you.
[00:36] Noor: Yeah hi all, thanks. So quick overview — Redwood supports Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. For private on-prem air-gapped installs we typically ship a customer-managed control plane or a completely offline bundle depending on policies. There are a few patterns: air-gapped with removable media updates, or locked VPC with restricted egress and a jumpbox for pulls.
[00:56] Thomas: Can you explain the removable media flow? Like, how do you get model updates in without internet?
[01:02] Noor: Sure. Common approach is: we provide signed artifact bundles — models, runtime binaries, and a verification manifest. Those artifacts are transferred via approved removable media, validated against an HSM or local KMS that holds the signing key, then installed using a sealed provisioning tool. The important bits are the signature verification, checksums, and audit trail.
[01:20] Dr. Chen: So who holds the signing keys? We cannot have Redwood private keys in our environment.
[01:25] Noor: Absolutely. Customer-held keys is the default for air-gapped. We support integrating with customer HSMs (YubiHSM, Thales, AWS CloudHSM when connected to an approved enclave) — or you can bring your own key material and we only sign during the build step but the final attest happens locally.
[01:40] Sarah: And what about attestation & chain-of-custody? Our audits will want to see exact who/when/media serial numbers.
[01:46] Noor: We add manifest metadata for media serial numbers and require operator signatures at each transfer step. We can log that to the local audit collector which you can forward to your SIEM.
[01:55] Thomas: Ok. On the hardware side, what's recommended — A100s vs H100s, and memory/PCIe needs? Procurement lead times are long.
[02:03] Noor: For 2026 models, H100 gives throughput gains for big seq lengths but it's more expensive and has tighter supply. A100 (80GB) remains a practical choice for many customers. We size based on expected qps, concurrency and seq length. For an initial pilot we often recommend a 2x A100 setup with NVMe local cache (4TB) and 100GbE between nodes.
[02:22] Evan: Note, we also provide quantized variants and can run some medium models on 1x A100 depending on latency needs.
[02:28] Thomas: Are there special kernel or driver constraints? We run RHEL with STIGs applied.
[02:32] Noor: We support RHEL/CentOS/Ubuntu; we publish a checklist of required kernel versions and driver stack. The runtime can work on locked-down kernels but we'll need the NVIDIA driver and CUDA toolchain versions (we hand you the exact validated combos in the reference arch). Some customers opt for our validated AMIs/IMs and then apply STIG overlays.
[02:49] Dr. Chen: What about crypto compliance? FIPS 140-2/3, HSM, KMS — do you have docs?
[02:54] Evan: Yes, we'll share SOC2 reports, our FIPS compatibility notes, and an offline deployment whitepaper. For key management the pattern is customer KMS/HSM. Redwood never keeps production keys for air-gapped installs.
[03:04] Thomas: Good. On licensing: if we have to sit on a private model bundle for months, what's the policy for patches/critical security fixes?
[03:12] Noor: We can push security advisories as metadata; patches are delivered as signed hotfix bundles. For air-gapped, we provide instructions for safe application and rollback. We also can support an on-site person or a secure remote session through your jumpbox if you allow temporary controlled egress.
[03:28] Sarah: Controlled egress is unlikely but we can discuss whitelisting a management host for a maintenance window.
[03:34] Evan: Many defense customers prefer a scheduled maintenance window where they'd physically attach media. We also have a certified partner who can facilitate onsite carries.
[03:42] Thomas: What about audit logs and integration with our Splunk instance?
[03:45] Noor: We can export structured audit logs; formats supported are syslog, JSON line files, or direct push to an on-prem Splunk HTTP collector during the maintenance window.
[03:55] Dr. Chen: Is there multi-tenant separation in the private deployment? We will host multiple tenant workloads internally and need RBAC and strong isolation.
[04:02] Noor: The private runtime supports namespace isolation, RBAC integrated with SAML/AD, and optional process-level sandboxing. We recommend separate node pools for high-assurance workloads.
[04:12] Evan: Also mention that you can pin model versions and have automatic fallback to a smaller, vetted model if a new model fails verification.
[04:20] Thomas: Hmm ok, fallback is nice. What about performance testing — can you run a benchmark in our environment?
[04:25] Noor: Yes, we do an onsite benchmark runbook. Typically we bring a small set of test artifacts and run generation/latency and throughput tests. For air-gapped we do it during the pilot install. We'll need an agreed prompt set.
[04:36] Thomas: Prompt set — yes we'll provide examples.
[04:38] Evan: Quick question on timelines: procurement lead times for GPUs — have you already ordered hardware or need Redwood's sizing to proceed?
[04:45] Carlos: Procurement here, lead times are about 12–16 weeks for H100s, 6–10 for A100 right now. If we lock a pilot spec we can start RFP next week.
[04:55] Noor: We'll send an initial hardware SOW that matches your expected concurrency. For a pilot we often do a smaller footprint to validate the flow.
[05:02] Sarah: On networking, we can't allow outbound DNS to internet. How does the runtime handle license checks?
[05:09] Noor: License checks are optional. For air-gapped we provide license tokens that are validated locally; or you can periodically revalidate via signed manifests. No outbound needed.
[05:18] Thomas: Are there any limitations around model families? Like some LLMs require specific drivers or CUDA features?
[05:24] Noor: Some optimizations (tensor cores, fp8) benefit H100; certain fused kernels are tuned per architecture. We publish a model compatibility matrix and recommended stack to avoid surprises.
[05:34] Dr. Chen: Pen testing and vulnerability scanning — do you allow scans of the runtime?
[05:39] Evan: We provide a pen test window and share our secure code review artifacts where possible. For air-gapped installs customers often run their own internal scans. We require a coordinated disclosure process.
[05:49] Dr. Chen: Ok, good. Also need to confirm supply chain provenance for binaries.
[05:53] Noor: We can provide SBOMs for our shipping artifacts and a signed chain-of-custody for each build.
[05:58] Thomas: Any example of previous air-gapped deployments for regulated orgs?
[06:02] Evan: Yes, we have a handful — governmental defense research labs and a life sciences customer. We can redact names but share architecture diagrams.
[06:10] Thomas: Makes sense. On the support side — what's the SLA if something goes down in an air-gapped env?
[06:16] Evan: Support tiers apply. For air-gapped we offer an enterprise support plan that includes 24x7 reached engineers, runbook access, and optional on-site support blocks. Response times depend on tier agreed in the contract.
[06:27] Sarah: On-site support requires cleared personnel—do you have personnel that can pass our background checks?
[06:31] Evan: We can arrange for partner personnel and also sign NDAs and meet clearance requirements where feasible; we'll follow up with our legal and security teams.
[06:39] Carlos: Pricing — does air-gapped cost more than standard dedicated?
[06:42] Evan: Typically yes because of extra engineering, packaging, and support overheads. We'll give a pilot price and a view for annual support.
[06:49] Noor: Also note that if you want on-prem control plane with no outbound, the operational burden shifts to you and we price accordingly.
[06:57] Thomas: How is monitoring done? We can't allow telemetry out.
[07:00] Noor: Monitoring can be local only, with push collectors you manage. Or you can allow a secure egress to send summarized telemetry to Redwood for proactive support.
[07:10] Dr. Chen: We are leaning toward no egress. We'll want local retention of all logs for 7 years and immutable WORM storage for audit trails. Can Redwood support that pattern?
[07:18] Evan: We can architect for local retention and WORM. Implementation details will depend on your storage backends; we'll include options in the follow-up doc.
[07:26] Thomas: About updates for models — how do you manage model licensing and IP? If we host open weights internally and fine-tune, what are the constraints?
[07:35] Noor: IP depends on model license. For open model weights you own the fine-tune outputs; we don't claim IP. For certain commercial models there may be license restrictions — we'll map those.
[07:45] Evan: We also provide tools for quantization so you can shrink model footprint for inference. That can help if your hardware budget is constrained.
[07:53] Thomas: Cool. Any blockers we should be aware of?
[07:56] Noor: The big ones: procurement lead times for H100, approval of offline update process by your auditors, and any policy that forbids removable media. If removable media is forbidden, we need a jumpbox-based sanctioned egress or an on-site partner.
[08:11] Sarah: Our change control currently forbids USB without express authorization. We can create a signed change for a pilot though.
[08:17] Dr. Chen: We also need to ensure the runtime meets our STIG baselines.
[08:21] Noor: We'll provide the checklist and a mapping to the runtime components.
[08:25] Evan: Quick logistics — we'd like to run an architecture deep-dive next week to review network diagrams and HSM options. Does Wednesday 11/25 work?
[08:33] Thomas: 11/25 is a holiday for us. How about Thursday 11/26?
[08:36] Evan: Works for us. We'll send a calendar invite.
[08:38] Carlos: Procurement needs a preliminary price for the pilot by end of next week to include in the RFP.
[08:42] Evan: Understood. We'll aim to send a pilot estimate and hardware sizing by 11/26.
[08:47] Noor: I'll take the hardware sizing action. Evan will send the security pack.
[08:51] Thomas: Any last questions?
[08:53] Dr. Chen: One more — integration with our SCAP-based baseline scanner — can Redwood produce results consumable by SCAP?
[08:59] Noor: Yes we can export relevant configs; we'll validate with your scanner during the deep-dive.
[09:06] Evan: Great. Thanks everyone, recap and next steps in the follow-up email.
[09:10] Sarah: Thanks.
[09:12] Thomas: Appreciate it.
[09:15] Speaker 1: (unlabeled) end call
[48:00] *call ended*
